For most of the twentieth century, film was treated as a disposable commodity rather than a cultural inheritance. Studios routinely melted down old prints to recover the silver in their emulsion, and the nitrate stock on which early cinema was shot decayed, caught fire, or was simply discarded once a film had finished its commercial run. By some estimates, the majority of movies made before 1930 no longer survive in any form. It was only in the latter half of the century, as scholars began to treat cinema as an art with a history worth preserving, that systematic archiving took hold.

Modern restoration is a painstaking and expensive craft. Technicians scan surviving prints frame by frame, then labour to remove scratches, correct faded colour, and reconstruct missing sequences from whatever fragments can be located in archives around the world. The goal, most restorers insist, is not to improve on the original but to return it as closely as possible to the state its makers intended. This principle is more contentious than it sounds. When a director's intentions were never documented, or when the only surviving print differs from the version audiences first saw, the restorer must make interpretive choices that shade into authorship.

Digital tools have made these choices sharper. Software can now invent plausible detail where none survives, smoothing a film into something crisper than any print ever looked. Purists warn that such enhancement risks producing a counterfeit, a version that never existed and that misleads viewers about how the film was actually experienced. Others counter that a pristine reconstruction, honestly labelled, does more to keep a film alive than a faithful copy no one will watch. The debate turns, ultimately, on whether preservation means guarding an object or sustaining an experience.

option.1: the discarding of prints once a film's commercial run had ended
option.2: the natural decay and flammability of the nitrate film stock
option.3: the transfer of prints to public archives for safekeeping
option.4: the melting of prints to recover silver from their emulsion

When streaming platforms overtook physical sales as the music industry's main source of revenue, they were hailed as the cure for piracy. Listeners who had grown used to downloading songs for free could now reach almost every recording ever made for a modest monthly fee, and the money, in theory, would flow back to the artists who made the music. A decade on, that promise looks more complicated. The industry's overall revenues have indeed recovered, but the way streaming distributes those revenues has provoked lasting resentment among the musicians it was meant to reward.

The core of the problem lies in how platforms pool and divide their subscription income. Rather than paying each listener's fee to the specific artists that listener actually plays, most services add all subscriptions into a single pot and share it out in proportion to each artist's share of total streams across the whole platform. Under this model, a handful of chart-topping performers capture the overwhelming majority of the pool, while the long tail of niche and emerging artists receives fractions of a cent per play. A musician with a devoted but small audience may find that their most loyal fans effectively subsidise stars those fans never listen to.

Reformers have proposed a user-centric model, in which each subscriber's fee is divided only among the artists that subscriber streams. Studies suggest this would modestly benefit smaller acts without greatly harming the biggest names. Yet the major labels, whose catalogues dominate the charts, have little incentive to champion a change that would trim their advantage, and the platforms are wary of the accounting complexity it would introduce. The technology that made abundance possible, it turns out, did nothing to settle the older question of how fairly its rewards should be shared.

option.1: They pool all fees and split them by each artist's share of total plays
option.2: They pay each subscriber's fee only to the artists that subscriber streams
option.3: They divide the income equally among every artist available on the service
option.4: They award fixed monthly sums to artists based on their chart positions

Video games tell stories in a way no older medium can: the audience does not merely watch events unfold but participates in bringing them about. A novelist decides exactly what happens on each page, and a filmmaker fixes every shot in a set order. A game designer, by contrast, must build a world in which the player's own choices help shape the tale. This shift from telling a story to enabling one is the defining challenge of narrative design in games.

The freedom that makes games distinctive also creates a tension. The more genuine control a player is given, the harder it becomes for designers to guarantee a satisfying dramatic shape. A story that can unfold in a thousand ways risks feeling shapeless, while one that funnels every player toward the same ending can make their choices feel like an illusion. Designers speak of this as the conflict between agency, the player's sense that their decisions matter, and authorship, the crafted arc that gives a story its emotional force.

Different games strike the balance differently. Some offer branching plots in which early decisions lead to genuinely distinct conclusions, at the cost of enormous extra writing that most players will never see. Others keep a fixed main storyline but let players colour it with optional side quests and small choices that alter tone rather than outcome. A few abandon authored plot almost entirely, scattering fragments of story through an environment for players to assemble in their own order and at their own pace.

None of these approaches is simply correct. Each trades away something to gain something else, and the right choice depends on what a particular game is trying to make its players feel. What unites them is the recognition that in an interactive medium, the player is never only an audience.

option.1: They rely on moving visual images instead of printed words to tell a story
option.2: Their plots are fixed in advance by a single author or a single director
option.3: The stories they tell are usually longer and more complex than those of films
option.4: The audience helps bring about events rather than only witnessing them

Because the systems learn from what most people already enjoy, they tend to funnel millions of users toward the same safe, familiar tracks. A modern blockbuster is assembled by hundreds of hands, its script revised by committee, its images finished by studios on three continents, its shape set as much by a release schedule as by any vision.
